# Book I, Proposition 19

*The greater angle is subtended by the greater side*

> In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/19-idea.svg" alt="The bigger angle (red) always looks across at the longer side (red), and the smaller angle (blue) at the shorter side (blue)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>The bigger angle (red) always looks across at the longer side (red), and the smaller angle (blue) at the shorter side (blue).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/19.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.19, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC greater than the angle BCA;

I say that the side AC is also greater than the side AB.

For, if not, AC is either equal to AB or less.

Now AC is not equal to AB;

for then the angle ABC would also have been equal to the angle ACB; [I. 5]

but it is not;

therefore AC is not equal to AB.

Neither is AC less than AB,

for then the angle ABC would also have been less than the angle ACB; [I. 18]

but it is not;

therefore AC is not less than AB.

And it was proved that it is not equal either.

Therefore AC is greater than AB.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop19.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop19.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side. -/
theorem Prop19 {A B C : Point} (hABC : Triangle A B C) (h : ∠ B C A < ∠ A B C) :
    ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖ := by
  -- Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC greater than the angle BCA;
  /- Euclid names the less angle BCA here and ACB below. They are one angle,
     read from either arm (`angle_symm`, System E's Metric 4). -/
  have hBCA_ACB : ∠ B C A = ∠ A C B := angle_symm hABC.ne₂₃ hABC.ne₁₃
  have hACB_ABC : ∠ A C B < ∠ A B C := hBCA_ACB ▸ h
  -- I say that the side AC is also greater than the side AB.
  -- For, if not, AC is either equal to AB or less.
  /- That a length not greater than another is equal to it or less is the tacit
     law of magnitudes `lt_trichotomy` (System E §3.5). -/
  have either : ¬ ‖A B‖ < ‖A C‖ → ‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ ∨ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ := by
    intro hnot
    rcases lt_trichotomy ‖A C‖ ‖A B‖ with hlt | heq | hgt
    · exact Or.inr hlt
    · exact Or.inl heq
    · exact absurd hgt hnot
  -- Now AC is not equal to AB;
  have not_equal : ‖A C‖ ≠ ‖A B‖ := by
    intro hAC_AB
    -- for then the angle ABC would also have been equal to the angle ACB; [I. 5]
    /- I.5 is stated with the equal sides produced, and here only the angles at
       the base are wanted, so `Prop5.base` produces AB and AC anywhere at all
       (Post. 2). -/
    have hABC_ACB : ∠ A B C = ∠ A C B := Prop5.base hABC hAC_AB.symm
    -- but it is not;
    /- It is greater: the hypothesis, with BCA read as ACB. -/
    have hne : ∠ A B C ≠ ∠ A C B := fun heq => Magnitude.ne_of_lt hACB_ABC heq.symm
    -- therefore AC is not equal to AB.
    exact hne hABC_ACB
  -- Neither is AC less than AB,
  have not_less : ¬ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖ := by
    intro hAC_AB
    -- for then the angle ABC would also have been less than the angle ACB; [I. 18]
    /- This is I.18 for the triangle ACB, whose side AB is the greater. It hands
       back the angle CBA, which is the angle ABC read the other way round. -/
    have hABC_ACB : ∠ A B C < ∠ A C B := by
      have hI18 : ∠ C B A < ∠ A C B := Prop18 hABC.acb hAC_AB
      rw [angle_symm hABC.ne₂₃.symm hABC.ne₁₂] at hI18
      exact hI18
    -- but it is not;
    /- It is greater, and a magnitude cannot be both less and greater than
       another (`lt_trans`, `lt_irrefl`). -/
    have hnot : ¬ ∠ A B C < ∠ A C B := fun hlt => lt_irrefl _ (lt_trans hlt hACB_ABC)
    -- therefore AC is not less than AB.
    exact hnot hABC_ACB
  -- And it was proved that it is not equal either.
  /- Both ways out are closed; Euclid's division is complete. -/
  have neither : ¬ (‖A C‖ = ‖A B‖ ∨ ‖A C‖ < ‖A B‖) := fun hor =>
    hor.elim not_equal not_less
  -- Therefore AC is greater than AB.
  /- Reductio ad absurdum: were AC not greater, the division above would make it
     equal or less, and it is neither. -/
  exact Classical.byContradiction fun hnot => neither (either hnot)
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**By means of division.** I.19 turns I.18 round, as I.6 turns I.5 round; Heath's rule for telling the pair apart, and Isaac Todhunter's aid to memory, are given under I.18. "Here, says Proclus (p. 318, 16–23), Euclid proves the impossibility 'by means of division' (ἐκ διαιρέσεως). This means simply the separation of different hypotheses, each of which is inconsistent with the truth of the theorem to be proved, and which therefore must be successively shown to be impossible" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 285). If AC is not greater than AB, it is equal to it or less. Euclid takes the division for granted; Lean names it, the tacit law of magnitudes `lt_trichotomy`, and closes it with `Classical.byContradiction`, as at the end of I.6.

**A purely logical deduction.** Heath: "This proposition, like I. 6, can be proved by merely logical deduction from I. 5 and I. 18 taken together, as pointed out by De Morgan." De Morgan takes three assertions X, Y, Z "of which it is the property that one or the other must be true, and one only", and three more, P, Q, R, of the same kind; if X brings P, Y brings Q and Z brings R, then "it follows that, when P is true, X is true, when Q is true, Y is true, when R is true, Z is true" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 284). Here X, Y, Z are AC equal to, greater than and less than AB, P, Q, R the same for the angles ABC and ACB, and I.5 and I.18 make the connexions. The Lean proof is his argument written out.

**What Lean made us say.** Euclid's hypothesis calls the less angle BCA and his argument calls it ACB, and Lean turns an angle round only when told to (`angle_symm`, System E, Metric 4). Euclid's "for then the angle ABC would also have been less than the angle ACB" is I.18 for the triangle ACB (`Triangle.acb`), which hands back the angle CBA, to be turned round once more. Each "but it is not" is a law of magnitudes: `Magnitude.ne_of_lt`, then `lt_trans` and `lt_irrefl`. As in I.18, our I.5 wants its equal sides produced (`Prop5.base`), so the proof uses Postulate 2 there; I.18 brings it in as well.

**The modern way.** Put B at (0, 0), C at (a, 0) and A at (x, y) with y > 0. Then cot B = x/y and cot C = (a − x)/y, so the angle at B is the greater exactly when x < a/2; and AC² − AB² = a(a − 2x), so AC is the greater exactly then too: I.18 and I.19 in one line.
